title: Modern Love - A Glance and a Rooster That Changed Everything
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads "A Glance and a Rooster That Changed Everything," a Modern Love column by Naomi Brynvillis, after announcing the September 19th closing ceremony for the dharma hall. Nomon frames the story with the six realms, the Manjushri koan, and Dogen's literal belief in rebirth, and asks how to engage strange material without flattening it into myth or psychology. The column follows a Haitian woman after the 2010 earthquake, when a Vaudoux priest prescribes a green onion, a wooden spoon, and a young rooster. A month later she meets Xander, a white aid worker, at a cholera treatment center. Nomon closes by asking how to hold all of it as stories, and opens the floor.

Also, I invite you, [unclear: "member thing is"] you can go to the dharma hall and use it individually.

You could chant a little bit.

It'd be good.
We put a lot into the place.
And that's available the whole month of September, and then we lose our occupancy.
So, saying goodbye, change.
And what a wonderful process we did together to make that decision.
It's so interesting to watch each of us, one by one, have to go through a little arc of what?
And I'm grateful we all came to agreement and consensus that it's just the thing to do next, and then eventually to have a new building.
Maybe we'll own it, whatever ownership really means.
Because it's problematic for us to go around talking to our donors about a permanent home, right?
What would that mean?

Some of you may have seen it, I've seen it.
It's not a new story.
It's a story from their column called Modern Love, so it's a love story.

The reason I want to read you this is that I was thinking about how so many of our koan stories and the sutra stories and so many Buddha stories, especially the Jataka stories, the tales before the Buddha was Buddha, are full of really far out stuff.
Things that we reference regularly, like the three realms of existence and the six levels of being and all this stuff, are actually pretty far out for us.
And maybe we see all that as cute, or myth, or cultural additions to the Buddha's pure understanding or something like that.
But some of them we can remap in a very useful everyday way as psychology, like the six realms.
That's the word I wanted a minute ago.
The six realms: you can be born to the hells or the hungry ghost realm or the animal realm or the human realm or the deva realm or the God realm.
Those are useful to think about as a moment-by-moment psycho-spiritual experience.
We and our circumstances manage to put ourselves into hell regularly, right?
And a lot of us are often hanging out in the hungry ghost world, always wanting more.
Capitalism depends on us being hungry ghosts.
And animals are simple and run on instinct.
How often do we do that?
The animal realm is like habit energy, just running on instinct, not thinking about what you're doing.
The early Buddhists didn't have the same green Sierra club idea of animals that we do.
And we know what the human realm is like, but from that frame we can appreciate it a little more.
What's great about the human realm is that we suffer, but we don't get so overwhelmed by suffering that we can't practice, and the suffering encourages us to practice.
Would you do this if you didn't have to?
I hope not.
Then we can bliss ourselves out and edge into the higher realms above the human realm, but then we find out those are unsatisfying.
Those aren't great.
And there's good psychological research that accords with this: people who don't have enough stress are not so happy either.
Life is too easy, lacking of challenge or something.
So anyway, we can think about a lot of these traditional teachings and the magical happenings as psychology or metaphor or myth.

Like the last koan, or a couple of koans ago, we were studying the way Manjushri shows up and snaps his fingers and sends this super-meditating woman to the heaven realm so he can walk around her and try to get her out of her samadhi, right?
It's really far out.
But I think if we do too much of that, making those stories tidy in our minds, "Oh, that's a cute myth," we may miss some of their meaning.
We may miss some of their truth.
And the Buddhists of the day, very likely, believed in those things very literally.
I remember Norman used to give talks about Dogen saying that Dogen didn't think this was just far out stuff.
He was in the middle of it.
Deeply true, deeply true.
So I think we would get more out of these teachings if we can also inhabit that level of it, the literal truth of it: that yes, when I die, I really could be reborn in some other realm.
And so I really have one more reason to keep upright and practice well and be ethical, so I can have the good fortune to be born again as a human and continue my bodhisattva work.

*A wooden spoon, a green onion, a pot with three legs, one bottle of Florida water, another of Champagne Andre, three candles, a bag of Poud Pajambe, don't cross here powder, and most important, a young rooster.*
I'm going to read that opening paragraph again because it doesn't hang together in your mind.

*A wooden spoon, a green onion, a pot with three legs, one bottle of Florida water, another of Champagne Andre, three candles, a bag of Poud Pajambe, don't cross here powder, and most important, a young rooster.
And I had been warned not to haggle over the rooster.
The merchant had five birds.
One was old and orange, three were adolescents, good for fighting but not much else.
The last was energetic, almost enthusiastic.
His red feathers looked gold in the sunlight.
How much for him, I asked.
She picked him up.
Three hundred Gordes, she said, a little over seven US dollars.
I paid her, tucked the bird under my arm and walked home.
It was April 2010.
Four months earlier an earthquake had killed hundreds of thousands of my fellow Haitians.*
*My family and I were homeless, sleeping behind a Mormon church, and I needed something to change.
Born in a town on Haiti's west coast, I had lived with my father and mother and seven siblings in Teguimi, the fisherman's quarter, until our house was washed away in a flood.
We slept on the floor of an aunt's house and then in a Baptist church.
My father was a good man who could never get ahead.
He left our family when I was 17.
My mother sold patties at a local school.
We survived on her daily wages, which I now know were less than one US dollar a day.
Finding money for school was an ordeal.
My sisters and I always wanted what we couldn't have, dolls, shoes, a backpack, a cell phone.
As the oldest sibling, I felt responsible for the others.*
*I moved to Port-au-Prince for college, which I attended when I could get the money to pay for it, and I was there when the earthquake struck, on a bus on my way to class.
I later learned that the school building collapsed, killing many of my classmates.
It then took me 12 hours to journey by foot through the ruined downtown to my uncle's house in Aviation, a neighborhood near the old airport.
My aunt was among the first to make camp on this old runway, where she was soon joined by thousands.
With the cell phone towers destroyed, I couldn't reach my family.
For five days, my mother thought I was dead.
It took me that long to travel the 67 kilometers, almost 42 miles, to Petit-Guaf.
The highway bridges were out, so we had to exit the buses each time, and wade to the other side.
I returned home to find my family sleeping in the street.*
*The next months were a nightmare.
I slept when I could, because I was hungry all the time.
Finally, in the depths of despair, I accompanied my friend to visit his spiritual guide, a Vaudoux priest in the town of Les Agnès.
As soon as he saw me, the priest knew what was wrong.
There's a shadow over your life.
What do you mean?
You must be first in a room, but you're last to be seen.
And so he wrote me a prescription, a green onion, a wooden spoon, and a young rooster, and told me to return when I'd gathered these important items.
When I asked my mother for the money, she said, I taught you the way of light.
This is the way of darkness.
As a devout Christian, she disapproves of Vaudoux.
I told her this was a deeper darkness than any I had ever faced, and that I was desperate for change.
And she finally gave me some money.*
*I filled the prescription and left for the priest's house with my sister.
The rooster was killed, and I was painted in his blood.
Afterward, I bathed in water infused with citrus leaves and Florida water.
When I offered my sister a piece of the cooked rooster, the priest said, No, you eat your fill before anyone else.
This accomplished, I was to go home and place a glass of water under the moon.
And then I must awake before anyone else, take the water in my mouth and spit in the cardinal directions.
The priest said I would then be washed and bright as a new penny.
He was right.*
*A month later when the whites arrived, aid workers, mostly from Europe, I was hired by Oxfam International to work as a hygiene specialist in the tent camps.
I made more money in one month doing this work than my mother had made in a year.
In October when the cholera epidemic started, I was transferred to the public health campaign and went into the camps with iodine tabs and bars of soap, teaching prevention and hygiene.
The hygienists were invited to tour the new cholera treatment center when it opened.
We found a series of tents set up over white gravel.
The incoming patients were stripped naked and sprayed with a blast of chlorine mist.*
*What I remember most about that day is not the smell of the place or even the morgue they were building.
It was the man I saw exiting the tent carrying a five gallon bucket.
He was handsome and enthusiastic, blonde into the sunlight.
I had not expected my rooster to be white.
We made eye contact.
That was all.
When I got home I told my sister I had seen my rooster and I was afraid I would never see him again.
But we did see each other again at a concert.
His name was Xander.
When he asked in Creole for my phone number I gave it to him.
And I woke the next day to find he had texted to say good morning.
Are you married?
I wrote no.
You have kids?
No.*
*My grandmother lived in the mountains.
Every few weeks she would come see my family in the city, bringing cocoa and coffee that she grew herself.
Everyone called her Madame Ticlis, or Mrs.
Smallseed, because she was only four feet ten.
When she came to see us over Christmas she was amazed to hear that I had gotten a job.
The job's not all she got, my mother said, mentioning my white boyfriend.
My grandmother said she never associated with them.
She had never associated with a white person outside of church.
And she didn't think they were all that friendly or good to be around.
But she returned a few weeks later with her own boyfriend, Emwa.
They'd been dating for 20 years and she said she wanted to hear the story.*
*And afterwards she insisted I bring Xander to their house for a visit.
Emwa was worried about the bad road and the long hike and the sorry state of the house, which had become infested with termites.
He truly cares for her, my grandmother said.
He will come.
This invitation was a test.
I was worried that Xander would fail, not wanting to trek into the mountains to visit my poor grandmother, but he said he would come.
On Sunday we left town in a little tap tap, a little truck taxi, and made our way to my grandmother's house.
I was ashamed of the dirt floor but Xander didn't seem to notice.*
*Our relationship deepened as the strife around us grew worse.
Cholera ravaged the tent camps.
Hundreds got sick.
Soon the morgue was filled.
Xander and I would meet for lunch, scrubbing our hands with Clorox soap, and then he would put his head in my lap.
I would play with his hair.
He extended his stay once and again until his visa was about to expire.
The first thing Xander did when he landed in Miami, before he called his own family, was to call me, and after that we spoke for hours every day.
Neighbors told me he would never return, that I was just a way to pass the time, but on the phone he asked if I wanted to come live with him.
I didn't know if he was serious.
I had never left Haiti or flown on a plane.
Why would he bring you to America, my friend said.
But he did return with a ring.
He got on one knee and asked me to marry him.*
*That was 10 years ago.
In American movies couples always seemed to have so much in common.
Xander and I couldn't even speak the same language.
He was still learning Creole when we met, and although I now speak English fluently I sure didn't then, but we know something that American cinema doesn't know.
Love has its own language.
I was born in the tropics, a black girl in the poorest country in the western hemisphere.
My husband was born in the north, a white man from the richest country on earth.
But from the day we first saw each other at the cholera treatment center, all that fell away and we were naked to each other as Naomi and Xander.

Ever since, for thousands of nights, we have said I love you to each other in the dark, and then we have fallen asleep marveling that it took an earthquake, an epidemic, a rooster and a passing glance to bring us together.*
That's the story.
So I'm seeing that far away from Buddhas appearing in the heavens to me.
Well, this is really worth thinking about.
I think we're always going to encounter everything we encounter with a habitual framework, our habitual way of looking at things.

So I think it's worthwhile to be deliberate and curious when we encounter something that's a little outside of our western scientific rational reality, whether it's a story from Haiti or an old Buddhist teaching.
What's an open, helpful, interesting way to engage with this story?
And in a way everything's stories, right?
We think it's all kind of real or something, but it's all stories: stories we remember, stories we tell, stories others tell us.
So how do we hold it all?
Let's put this off us, and we'll just stop the recording and open the floor.
Have any thoughts about all this?
